claims.text: Standard zirconium-alloy nuclear-fuel cladding has a native surface that is susceptible to oxidation.
A sub-micron nanocrystalline Al2O3 coating can be deposited conformally on zirconium-alloy cladding by atomic layer deposition.
Accident-relevant oxidation conditions include steam exposure at approximately 1000–1200°C.
The proposed benefit is expected under service-relevant mechanical stresses.
ALD alumina will form a dense and continuous layer on the zirconium-alloy substrate.
The alumina layer will adhere well to the zirconium substrate during high-temperature exposure.
A dense, continuous alumina layer will retard oxygen transport to the zirconium alloy.
Alumina has inherently low oxygen diffusivity.
Alumina is chemically inert under the proposed exposure conditions.
At high temperature, the alumina coating forms a thermodynamically stable protective layer.
Limiting oxygen transport through the alumina layer will slow oxidation kinetics of the underlying zirconium alloy.
Slower oxidation kinetics will delay formation of detrimental oxide scales on the zirconium alloy.
Relative to uncoated cladding under identical steam-oxidation conditions, coated cladding will have a lower oxidation rate.
The lower oxidation rate will be observable as reduced weight gain.
The lower oxidation rate will be observable as a thinner oxide scale.
The coated cladding will retain the mechanical integrity required for reactor service.
The coated cladding will retain the neutron transparency required for reactor service.
The oxidation benefit depends on the alumina coating remaining intact and adherent during exposure.
Performance improvement may not persist under conditions significantly beyond typical operational or accident scenarios.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant oxidation reduction, or failure of coating integrity under simulated service stresses, would falsify the hypothesis.
